Sources and sinks: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon MSK (Apache Kafka), Amazon S3, and others through Flink connectors; write results to Kinesis, Amazon Data Firehose, S3, OpenSearch Service, databases, or SageMaker Feature Store.
Stateful processing: Flink keeps state (counts, windows, last values) per key, so it can compute rolling averages, sessions, and features over time windows for training and inference.
Event time and windows: tumbling, sliding, and session windows based on when events happened, handling late data.
Calling a model: the DataStream API can call an external endpoint asynchronously, for example an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint or Amazon Bedrock, to score each event.

Studio notebooks: interactive SQL, Python, or Scala queries on live streams for exploration and dashboards; a notebook can be promoted to a long-running application. For production pipelines with version control and CI/CDCI/CD (Continuous integration and continuous delivery)Practices in which every code change is built and tested automatically (continuous integration) and kept ready to release, often deploying it automatically through a pipeline (continuous delivery or deployment).Glossary entryClose, build the application in an IDE.

Managed Apache Flink for stateful, real-time stream processing in Java, Scala, Python, or SQL.
Reads Kinesis and Kafka, writes to streams, S3, Firehose, OpenSearch, and feature stores.
Checkpoints and snapshots protect state; automatic scaling adjusts parallelism.
Pay for KPUs per hour; monitor lag (millisBehindLatest), backpressure, and checkpoints in CloudWatch.

paragraphs: Managed Apache Flink for real-time stream processing: applications in Java, Scala, Python, or SQL, Studio notebooks, sources and sinks such as Kinesis and Amazon MSK, checkpoints and snapshots, scaling, streaming feature engineering and inference, security, and cost.

Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink runs Apache Flink applications that process streaming data in real time, written in Java, Scala, Python, or SQLSQL (Structured Query Language)The standard language for querying and changing data in relational databases. Analytics services such as Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift also use SQL.Glossary entryClose. AWS provides the infrastructure: compute, parallelism, automatic scaling, Availability ZoneAZ (Availability Zone)An isolated location within an AWS Region, made up of one or more data centers with their own power, cooling, and networking. The AZs in a Region are linked by fast, low-latency connections, so spreading resources across them protects against the failure of one site.Glossary entryClose failoverFailoverSwitching automatically to a standby resource when the primary one fails, such as a standby database in Amazon RDS or a backup site chosen by Route 53 failover routing.Glossary entryClose, and backups of application state as checkpoints and snapshots. You use Flink's own APIsAPI (Application programming interface)A defined way for one program to ask another for data or actions, such as a set of HTTPS requests and responses. Every AWS service is controlled through its API, which the console, the CLI, and the SDKs call for you.Glossary entryClose (DataStream, Table API, and Flink SQL), sources, and sinks as you would on your own cluster. The service was previously named Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics for Apache Flink.

Choose it when a question asks to transform, aggregate, or enrich a stream continuously with statefulStatefulKeeping track of earlier requests or connections. A stateful firewall, such as a security group, remembers allowed connections and lets their return traffic back in automatically.Glossary entryClose logic: windows, joins between streams, real-time features for MLML (Machine learning)Software that learns patterns from example data to make predictions or decisions, instead of following rules written by hand. A model is first trained on data, then used to make predictions on new data, which is called inference.Glossary entryClose, anomaly detection, or calling a model for each event (MLA-C02 tasks 1.1.4 and 1.2.3).
The application runs with an IAM role for its sources and sinks; connect it to your VPC to reach private resources such as an MSK cluster; data is encrypted in transit and state is encrypted at rest.

Checkpoints are taken automatically so an application recovers from failures without losing or duplicating state; snapshots are backups you create or take on update and can restore from. The service handles AZ failover.

Throughput depends on parallelism: the number of parallel tasks. Automatic scaling raises parallelism with CPU load; set parallelism per task to match the number of Kinesis shards or Kafka partitions. Watch for backpressure and checkpoint duration.

You pay for Kinesis Processing Units (KPUs), units of compute and memory, per hour while the application runs, plus storage for running state and backups. Right-size parallelism and stop development applications when idle.

Amazon CloudWatch shows metrics such as records in and out, millisecond latencyLatencyThe time between sending a request and receiving the response, usually measured in milliseconds. Distance and processing add to it; caching and serving users from nearby locations reduce it.Glossary entryClose, backpressure, checkpoint size and duration, and millisBehindLatest (how far behind the stream the application is); application logs go to CloudWatch Logs.
